title: Parliament should pass the 2026 budget's restriction of negative gearing to newly built homes
oneLiner: The policy is now a bill before the Senate: negative gearing for new builds only from July 2027, existing investors grandfathered, and a reworked capital gains discount alongside it.
body: The 12 May 2026 budget restricted negative gearing to newly built residential property for investments made after budget night, with effect from 1 July 2027, and replaced the 50 per cent capital gains discount with an inflation-based discount and a 30 per cent floor. Anyone using the concessions before budget night keeps them. A Senate inquiry took evidence in June 2026.
contextBackground:
Australia is unusual in letting rental losses offset wage income without limit. With the capital gains discount introduced in 1999, this made a loss-making rental a tax-effective way to hold an appreciating asset ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_gearing_in_Australia)). The concession was quarantined in 1985 and restored in 1987; a new-builds-only policy lost the 2016 and 2019 elections; the prime minister ruled out changes during the 2025 campaign.

In February 2026 Treasury was [reported to be modelling options](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-02-27/labor-not-ruling-out-negative-gearing-changes/106395074). The May budget adopted new-builds-only with grandfathering. Treasury's secretary told the Senate the measures mainly [change who owns housing](https://thenightly.com.au/politics/jenny-wilkinson-says-labor-tax-changes-will-reallocate-housing-as-investors-pull-back-c-22353594) rather than how much is built; the property industry's commissioned modelling forecasts higher rents and fewer homes.
contextDisagreement: Economists agree the concession pushes prices up at the margin and that the effect is modest. The live dispute is rents: Treasury puts the rise at under $2 a week, the industry's modelling at about $9. Behind that is a design fight over indefinite grandfathering, which keeps the concession alive for decades on existing stock.

timeline.text: Rental losses are quarantined so they can only be offset against rental income.
Quarantining is reversed after rents rise in Sydney and Perth.
The capital gains tax discount is introduced, increasing the appeal of loss-making property investment.
A federal opposition takes a new-builds-only policy to two elections and loses both.
During the election campaign the prime minister rules out changes to negative gearing.

timeline.label: Feb 2026
timeline.text: Treasury is reported to be modelling a two-property cap and a lower capital gains discount; the government does not rule out change.

timeline.label: 12 May 2026
timeline.text: The budget restricts negative gearing to new builds from 1 July 2027 and replaces the 50 per cent CGT discount, grandfathering existing investors.

timeline.label: Jun 2026
timeline.text: The bill is debated in the House and examined by a Senate inquiry; industry modelling and Treasury disagree on rents.

otherClaim.title: The large majority of investor housing loans finance established dwellings rather than new construction

claimItself.title: The large majority of investor housing loans finance established dwellings rather than new construction
claimItself.oneLiner: If the concession is meant to add rental supply, most of it is going to homes that already exist.
claimItself.body: Lending data published monthly by the Bureau of Statistics shows investor loans for the construction or purchase of new dwellings are a small fraction of total investor lending. Most investor borrowing buys existing homes, where it competes directly with owner-occupiers.

otherClaim.title: Limiting negative gearing to new builds would make housing materially more affordable

claimItself.title: Limiting negative gearing to new builds would make housing materially more affordable
claimItself.oneLiner: Removing the tax advantage for investors in existing homes would take heat out of the market first-home buyers compete in.
claimItself.body: Investors and first-home buyers bid for the same established dwellings. Removing a concession available only to one side would, proponents argue, shift enough demand to make a visible difference to prices and to who wins at auction.

otherClaim.title: The tax system should not treat buying a second home more favourably than buying a first

claimItself.title: The tax system should not treat buying a second home more favourably than buying a first
claimItself.oneLiner: A fairness claim, independent of any price effect.
claimItself.body: An owner-occupier cannot deduct mortgage interest; an investor can deduct it against wages. Proponents argue that whatever the market effect, a tax system that rewards the purchase of a second home over a first is backwards.

otherClaim.title: Winding back negative gearing would push rents up as investors leave the market

claimItself.title: Winding back negative gearing would push rents up as investors leave the market
claimItself.oneLiner: Fewer landlords means fewer rentals, and fewer rentals means higher rents.
claimItself.body: If the after-tax return on rental property falls, some investors will sell and fewer will buy. Opponents of reform argue that the resulting withdrawal of rental stock would raise rents for the tenants the policy is meant to help.

claimItself.title: New housing completions have not kept pace with population growth in Australia's largest cities over the past decade
claimItself.oneLiner: Dwellings built per new resident have fallen, and vacancy rates in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth sit near record lows.
claimItself.body: Completions peaked around 2017 and fell through the pandemic as costs rose and builders failed, while population growth resumed at pace. The national housing agency's projections show a cumulative shortfall against household formation through the second half of the decade.

claimItself.oneLiner: Tax office data is cited to show the concession is used mainly by middle earners, not the wealthy.
claimItself.body: Tax statistics show that the majority of individuals reporting a net rental loss have taxable incomes under $100,000. Defenders of the concession cite this to argue it is a middle-class saving tool rather than a tax break for the rich.

claimItself.title: Grandfathering existing investors indefinitely keeps the concession alive on most of the housing stock for decades
claimItself.oneLiner: An argument that the bill is too timid, made from the reform side.
claimItself.body: Because anyone negatively gearing before budget night keeps the concession for as long as they hold the property, the change bites only on future purchases of established homes. A government member in the House debate urged phasing out the deduction on existing properties over seven years instead.
